say: Welcome to Puzzle Day! Today there is no new topic. Instead, you get the puzzles that mathematicians love, the ones where you do not know how to start.
Good problem solvers are not people who know every answer. They know how to START. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100. I will give you one clue at a time. After each clue, cross out every number it cannot be.
Clue 1: I am a 2-digit number. Which numbers can you cross out straight away?
Look at the four puzzle cards. Which one do you think will be hardest? Write the letter in the corner of your whiteboard. We will check at the end.
stuck: Stuck on card A: try 10 × 11, then a bigger pair. Is the answer too big or too small?
Stuck on card B: what if all 10 bugs were beetles? How many legs would that be?
Stuck on card C: start at 43 and undo the last thing first.
Finished early: make up a new card for one of the stations.

say: “Two next-door numbers multiply to 342. I estimate: 20 × 20 is 400, too big. Try 17 × 18 = 306, too small. 18 × 19 = 342. My table tells me which way to go after each try.”

“15 bicycles and tricycles with 38 wheels. Suppose they are ALL bicycles: 30 wheels. I am 8 wheels short. Each time I swap a bicycle for a tricycle I get 1 more wheel. So I swap 8: 8 tricycles and 7 bicycles. Check: 14 + 24 = 38.”
“Siti spent half, then $4, and had $11. I start at the end and undo each step, last one first: add the 4 back, $15; double it, $30. Check forwards: half of 30 is 15, take 4 is 11.”

do: Ask: “What is your way in? Why did you choose it?”
Ask: “Does your answer fit EVERY fact in the question? Show me.”
Ask: “Could there be another answer? How do you know?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Make a table and try a number. Was it too big or too small?”
Hint 2: “What if they were all the same? How far off are you?”
Hint 3: “Start at the end and undo, last step first.”

say: “Which way in did you use most today?”
“If you would like to, pick one puzzle and tell us your way in, in two sentences. Volunteers first. You can pass.”
ask: “Which way in did you use most today?”
Open answers. Listen for the name of the strategy (guess and check, suppose, work backwards, logic grid, draw it) and a check against every fact.

say: “You are real inquirers now: you can start a problem you have never seen before.”
Certificates and stamped journals go out after the lesson, each with a personal sentence you wrote before it (never read out in class).

p4l10-title.note: Objective: Choose a way into a non-routine problem (guess and check with a table, suppose they are all the same, work backwards, a logic grid, draw it) and use it on competition-style puzzles, checking every answer against every fact. Thinking strategies today: GUESS AND CHECK WITH A TABLE, SUPPOSE (heads and legs), WORK BACKWARDS, LOGIC GRID, DRAW IT. Materials: Four puzzle cards (A to D) for the explore stations, mini whiteboards, counters or cubes, certificates, stamps. Online: pairs go to breakout rooms with one puzzle card each and report back; the tutor ticks and crosses the logic grid on the slide as children call out. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 2-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 24.5 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 24.5 to 31 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 31 to 34.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 34.5 to 76: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 34.5 to 51, check together 51 to 52.5, short teaching before page 2 52.5 to 56, page 2 on your own 56 to 73 (the last 2 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 73 to 76. Talk time 76 to 80.5 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 80.5 to 85. Looking back 85 to 87.5 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). Certificates and goodbye 87.5 to 90 (whole group, no per-child comments). Pairs: Q1a, Q2. Then Q3 alone. After Q3 choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today you choose the tool. Point at the row of eight tools on page 1 of the workbook.

p4l10-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 10 legs, then 12 legs. Changing a duck into a rabbit adds 2 legs. 2) 3 rabbits (and 5 ducks): 5 × 2 + 3 × 4 = 22. Suppose all 8 are ducks: 16 legs, 6 too few; each rabbit instead of a duck adds 2 legs, so 3 rabbits. A GOOD REASON: Pick a way in: guess and check with a table, suppose they are all the same, or work backwards from the end. Then check every fact. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "Pairs: Q1a, Q2. Then Q3 alone. After Q3 choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l10-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Who am I? Children have a 1 to 100 grid (or a whiteboard list). Click one clue at a time; after each, children cross out every number that no longer fits. Clicks: clue 1, clue 2, the 7 times table shades (14, 21, 28 … 98), clue 3, 28 and 91 are circled, clue 4, the answer, the question. Clue 3 check: 1 + 4, 2 + 1, 2 + 8 = 10 ✓, 3 + 5, 4 + 2, 4 + 9, 5 + 6, 6 + 3, 7 + 0, 7 + 7, 8 + 4, 9 + 1 = 10 ✓, 9 + 8. So 28 and 91; clue 4 leaves 91. Clue 2 did the most work: it left only 13 numbers. Say it as a statement; no follow-up question.

p4l10-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Three questions from earlier lessons, about 30 seconds each. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. 1) 9:24: the first common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24 (Factor Hunters). 2) 46 000: the hundreds digit is 6, so round up (Big Number Puzzles). 3) 24 ÷ 4 = 6, 6 × 3 = 18 (Fraction Frontier). The other two (0.6 × 4 = 2.4; turn clockwise from N to SW, 225°) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l10-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 21.5. Pairs do two live cards, A then B (online: one breakout room for the whole explore, about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer). Cards C and D are take-home (★): they are the first Think harder tasks to try at home. Full cards: A) Two next-door numbers multiply to make 210. What are they? B) Spiders have 8 legs and beetles have 6 legs. 10 bugs have 68 legs altogether. How many spiders? C) I double a number and add 7. I get 43. What is my number? D) Ali, Mei and Ravi each have a different pet: a cat, a dog and a fish. Ali's pet has no fur. Mei's pet does not bark. Who has which pet? Answers: A) 14 and 15. B) 4 spiders and 6 beetles. C) 18. D) Ali fish, Mei cat, Ravi dog. Hands-on is about 6 minutes for the two live cards. Do not teach the methods yet: let pairs try their own way. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if 10 bugs have 65 legs? Could that happen? Why or why not? Answer: No. Spiders have 8 legs and beetles 6: both are even numbers, so the total number of legs is always even, and 65 is odd.

p4l10-explore2.note: Minutes 21.5 to 24.5. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather pairs and collect ways of starting. Two debrief questions only: write them on the board in children's words ("I guessed and changed it", "I pretended they were all beetles", "I started at 43"). Answers: 1) Suppose all 10 are beetles: 60 legs, 8 short; each spider instead of a beetle adds 2 legs, so 4 spiders. Or guess and check with a table. 2) Open. The third question (could any card have two answers?) is not asked: A has only 14 × 15 = 210 and C undoing gives one number. The next slides name the four ways in.

p4l10-teach1.note: Teach: the idea and why. "Mathematicians do not know the answer straight away. They know ways to START." Click each card and link it to the explore stations: A was guess and check, B was suppose, C was work backwards, D was a logic puzzle. A puzzle can often be started more than one way: B can also be done by guess and check. The next slides show each way in action, with new numbers.

p4l10-we1.note: Click: each reason on the right, then its row in the table. Think-aloud: "I could guess at random, but a table is smarter: every try tells me whether to go up or down. 20 × 20 is 400, so the numbers are a bit less than 20. 20 × 21 = 420, too big. 17 × 18 = 306, too small. So 18 × 19: 18 × 19 = 342." Worked check: 18 × 19 = 18 × 20 − 18 = 360 − 18 = 342. Worksheet Q1 uses a different number.

p4l10-we2.note: Click the steps, then 8 cycles get a third wheel, then the answer. Think-aloud: "Two facts: 15 cycles and 38 wheels. I keep the 15 and pretend they are all bicycles. That gives 30 wheels: 8 too few. Every time I change a bicycle into a tricycle I add exactly 1 wheel, so I change 8 of them." Check BOTH facts: 7 + 8 = 15 cycles, 7 × 2 + 8 × 3 = 38 wheels. Point out: for chickens and goats, each swap adds 2 legs, so you divide the shortfall by 2. Worksheet Q2 is a heads-and-legs puzzle.

p4l10-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) All ducks: 20 legs, 8 short, each cow adds 2: 4 cows (and 6 ducks; 12 + 16 = 28). b) All 10¢: 120¢, 60¢ short, each 20¢ adds 10¢: six 20¢ and six 10¢ (120 + 60 = 180). c) All bicycles: 18 wheels, 8 short, each car adds 2: 4 cars and 5 bicycles (16 + 10 = 26).

p4l10-we3.note: Think-aloud: "I know the END, $11, not the start. So I walk backwards through the machine, undoing each step, LAST step first. She took away $4, so I add it back: $15. She halved her money, so I double: $30." Check forwards: half of $30 is $15, $15 − $4 = $11 ✓. Common mistakes: undoing in the wrong order (11 × 2 = 22, 22 + 4 = 26: check forwards and it fails), or taking away 4 again. Worksheet Q3 has three steps to undo.

p4l10-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Guessing at random instead of using a table, so each try does not tell them whether to go up or down. (2) Working backwards but doing the same operation again (taking away 4 instead of adding 4), or undoing the steps in the wrong order. (3) Queues: adding the two positions (7th and 12th makes 19) and counting the person twice; logic puzzles: stopping before every clue has been used.

p4l10-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 34.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. 3 chickens and 2 goats: 6 + 8 = 14 stamps. 5 animals with 16 legs: all chickens is 10 legs, 6 short, each goat adds 2, so 3 goats and 2 chickens (12 + 4 = 16 ✓). Online: children stamp or clap in place on camera.

p4l10-ws1.note: Minutes 34.5 to 51. Pairs do Q1a and Q2 (about 9 minutes of work). Q1b (all the ways to buy pens and notebooks) is a ★ take-home question. Q3 (working backwards) is the first question each child does on their own, at the start of page 2 time; its answer is checked with page 2. Walk around. Ask "What is your way in?" and "Does it fit every fact?" before giving any help. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "Pairs: Q1a, Q2. Then Q3 alone. After Q3 choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l10-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains their way in. Q1a: 20 × 20 = 400 and 25 × 25 = 625, so try 23 × 24 = 552 ✓. Q1b: money left for pens with 1 to 7 notebooks is $43, $36, $29, $22, $15, $8, $1; only $36 (9 pens) and $8 (2 pens) can be paid with $4 pens. Q2: 50 − 36 = 14, 14 ÷ 2 = 7 goats; check 11 × 2 + 7 × 4 = 50. Q2c: all motorcycles 48 wheels, 22 short, 11 cars.

p4l10-teachlogic.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 is a 4 by 4 grid). Click: step 1, then its ticks and crosses; step 2, then its marks; step 3, then the last tick. Think-aloud: "Each person has exactly one sport, and each sport has exactly one person. So when I tick a box, I can cross out the rest of that row AND that column." Answer: Ben badminton, Siti swimming, Ravi football. On the worksheet, children write ✓ for yes and X for no.

p4l10-teachqueue.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Ask first: "Is it 13?" Many children add 5 + 8. Draw it: click the brackets, then the steps. Think-aloud: "If Ali is 5th, there are 4 people in front of him. If he is 8th from the back, there are 7 behind him. Ali himself is 1. 4 + 1 + 7 = 12." Quick check on the picture: count the circles: 12. Going the other way: 30 people, Mei 11th from the front: 19 behind her, so she is 20th from the back (30 − 11 + 1).

p4l10-teachages.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Ask first: "In 4 years, how much older is the TOTAL?" Many say 4: but two people each get 4 years older, so the total grows by 8. Click step 1, the bars, steps 2 and 3, the answer. Think-aloud: "The twice-as-old fact is about the future, so I draw the bars in 4 years: Mei one bar, her aunt two bars, 48 altogether. 48 ÷ 3 = 16. That is Mei in 4 years, so now she is 12." Common mistake: forgetting to go back to NOW at the end.

p4l10-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who still adds the two queue positions, and who forgets to go back to NOW in Q6. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Do question 3 first, then Q4 and Q5. Q6 is a choice for the end. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 2 minutes of this block (minute 71 to 73) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l10-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3a (done first on their own): 30 + 5 = 35, 35 − 9 = 26, 26 × 2 = 52; check forwards 26, 35, 30 ✓. Q3b: 21 × 2 = 42, 42 + 18 = 60, 60 ÷ 3 = 20. Q4: clue 1 gives Ali and Siti the two rice dishes; clue 2 means Ali has nasi lemak, so Siti has chicken rice; Ben and Mei have laksa and prata, and clue 3 gives Ben laksa, Mei prata. Q5a: 6 in front + Mei + 11 behind = 18. Q5b: 14 people behind Ben, so he is 15th from the back (20 − 6 + 1). Q6: in 5 years the total is 50 + 10 = 60; father 3 bars, Ben 1 bar: 4 bars = 60, 1 bar = 15; Ben will be 15, so he is 10 now. Check: 10 + 40 = 50; 15 and 45, and 45 = 3 × 15 ✓.

p4l10-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 7 tricycles (and 13 bicycles). All bicycles: 40 wheels, 7 short, each swap adds 1. 2) 24 and 26 3) $51 (18 × 2 = 36, 36 + 15 = 51) 4) Ali 11, Ben 10, Siti 9, Mei 8. Ali is 2 more than Siti, so (Siti, Ali) is (8, 10) or (9, 11). Mei is younger than both Siti and Ben. If Siti were 8, Mei would have to be younger than 8. So Siti is 9 and Ali is 11, and Mei is 8. Ben is the one left, 10.

p4l10-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q6. Answers: 1) (a) 8 tables seat 6 (and 7 seat 4). (b) Fewest 60 (all seat 4), most 90 (all seat 6). (c) No: every table seats an even number of people, so the total is even and 77 is odd. The diagrams that follow show part (a). 2) 32 stickers.

p4l10-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: In Q1, what if every table seated 4? In Q2, where do we know the number for sure? Which way in fits each puzzle? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l10-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1 is a heads-and-legs puzzle in disguise: tables are the heads, seats are the legs. Q2: "half and 2 more" is undone in two steps, last first: add the 2 back (that is the half she kept), then double. Many children add 2 and then halve, or take 2 away: check forwards to catch it. 32: Ali gets 16 + 2 = 18, 14 left. Ben gets 7 + 2 = 9, 5 left ✓.

p4l10-gap-time.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM time (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Timetables, trying both orders"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: List every way. SAY: There are only two orders. Try the first order, write the clock times down the page, then try the other order. ASK: In the library-first order, what time does he reach the post office? Does it work? LISTEN FOR: Library first: arrives 3:10, leaves 3:20, reaches the post office at 3:35, too late. Post office first: 3:00, leaves 3:10, library at 3:25, leaves 3:35, home at 4:05. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) The post office first. (b) 4:05 pm. WHY: Post office first: arrive 3:00, leave 3:10, walk 15 minutes to the library at 3:25 (open), leave 3:35, walk 30 minutes home: 4:05 pm. Library first fails because he arrives at the post office at 3:35. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Change the post office closing time to 3:40 pm. Which orders work now, and which gets Kumar home sooner? Answer: Both orders work. Post office first gets home at 4:05 pm; library first: library 3:10 to 3:20, post office 3:35 to 3:45, home 4:05 pm. They tie at 4:05 pm.

p4l10-gap-dice.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM dice (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Smallest and largest totals"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: List every way. SAY: Do not roll anything. Ask what the lowest face and the highest face on one die are, then think about 4 dice. ASK: Can she get every total from 4 to 24? How can you tell? LISTEN FOR: Smallest 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, largest 6 + 6 + 6 + 6. Listen for "change one die by 1 at a time", which gives every total in between. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 4. (b) 24. (c) 3 and 25 are impossible. WHY: 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 × 6 = 24. Starting at 4 you can raise one die by 1 at a time up to 24, so every total from 4 to 24 can be made. 3 is below 4 and 25 is above 24. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Siti rolls 5 dice and adds the scores. Find the least and the greatest total possible. Answer: 5 and 30.

p4l10-gap-stages.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM stages (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Counting in two stages"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: List every way. SAY: Draw 4 boxes for the tops. Under each one, show 3 skirts. How many top-and-skirt pairs is that? ASK: How many outfits use the red top with the green skirt? What do you do with that number? LISTEN FOR: 4 × 3 = 12 pairs, times 2 hats = 24. Listen for "multiply the choices". For (b) the red-green pair has 2 outfits (one for each hat); 24 − 2 = 22. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 24 outfits. (b) 22 outfits. WHY: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. The red top with the green skirt can go with either hat, so 2 outfits are removed: 24 − 2 = 22. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): A bus route has 3 ways from the depot to the market and 4 ways from the market to the harbour. Find the number of routes from the depot to the harbour through the market. Answer: 12 routes.

p4l10-talk.note: Minutes 76 to 80.5. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Listen for the name of the strategy (guess and check, suppose, work backwards, logic grid, draw it) and a check against every fact. Only if volunteers dry up: "Which puzzle could be started in two different ways?" (heads and legs: suppose, or guess and check with a table). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l10-exit.note: Minutes 80.5 to 85. Answer: 5 goats (and 7 ducks). Suppose all ducks: 24 legs, 10 short, each goat adds 2 legs: 5 goats. Check: 14 + 20 = 34. Accept a guess-and-check table too. Extension: write your own heads-and-legs puzzle with exactly one answer and swap with a partner.

p4l10-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 87.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 87.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.

p4l10-end.note: Minutes 87.5 to 90 (2.5 minutes, whole group, no per-child comments). Certificates and stamped journals are posted or sent after the lesson, each with a personal sentence the tutor wrote before the lesson. Live: three volunteers each name one puzzle and one way in (about 20 seconds each), then say one sentence about the group, then goodbye. Give parents the one-page summary from the tutor guide.
